column3: It repeats the focus's closure after another prophetic narrative: an event is a sign although most people do not believe.
Moses's purpose of abundant praise belongs to his mission but does not explain the sign or the majority's nonbelief.
The identical narrative closure independently reinforces that a visible sign does not make the majority believe.
The same closure after Lot's narrative preserves the focus's sign-and-majority-nonbelief pattern.
The immediately following declaration that the Lord is Mighty and Merciful completes the focus's narrative closure and reassigns might.
It calls the aftermath of Lot's story a sign for believers, supporting the distinction between visible evidence and receptive belief.
The identical closure after Shuayb's story directly reiterates the focus's sign and majority-nonbelief formula.
Continued remembrance by Moses concerns his mission's devotion, not the reception of the sign by Pharaoh's majority.
Creation is called a sign for believers, a broad parallel to the focus without its narrative rejection or majority contrast.
The same closure after the sea deliverance directly repeats the focus's sign and majority-nonbelief formula.
God's sight of Moses supports the mission setting only indirectly and adds nothing about signs or nonbelief.
Its statement that most callers do not understand has no material connection to a sign being rejected.
The identical closure after Thamud's punishment reiterates the focus's sign and majority-nonbelief pattern.
This companion declaration after the repeated closure identifies the Lord, not the opponent, as Mighty and Merciful.
Provision is a sign for believing people, but the verse lacks the focus's narrative of a majority refusing belief.
The identical closure after Hud's people directly reiterates that the narrated outcome is a sign despite majority nonbelief.
It states that only those who believe in God's signs can truly hear, explaining why a sign need not compel a closed receiver.
Its observation that people believe little broadly echoes scarce belief but does not concern the focus's sign.
It names narrated events as signs and tests, clarifying that human response is part of what the focus's sign exposes.
The prayer for forgiveness and mercy does not illuminate the focus's sign or majority nonbelief.
The command for frequent remembrance is unrelated to the evidentiary sign and rejection in the focus.
It calls Pharaoh's fate a lesson for the reverent, a close historical parallel to the focus's narrated sign.
This companion declaration after the repeated closure confirms the Lord's might and mercy as the focus's next verse does.
Safety from fear does not address signs, Pharaoh, or the majority's response to evidence.
The abandoned homes left by wrongdoing are an enduring visible sign, paralleling the focus's use of narrated ruin as evidence.
The same Quran brings mercy to believers and increasing loss to wrongdoers, showing that reception determines a sign's effect.
Most people lacking knowledge is only a broad majority contrast and does not involve the focus's sign or response.
It directly states that most people will not believe despite the messenger's concern, reinforcing the focus's majority contrast.
The rescue of Shuayb's believers and destruction of wrongdoers supplies a narrative outcome akin to the focus's sign-bearing history.
It makes denial of God's signs the stated cause of lasting punishment, supplying the judicial consequence of the focus's nonbelief.
Even a complete recitation by a foreign-language messenger does not produce belief, directly explaining the focus's majority nonbelief.
This companion declaration after the Noah closure mirrors the Lord's might and mercy that immediately follows the focus.
It contrasts belief and obstruction among recipients of revelation, but lacks the focus's sign and majority formulation.
The attempted burning and Abraham's rescue become signs for believers, a historical sign parallel with a different response pattern.
Moses calls his people to trust God, providing a believing counter-response within the Pharaoh narrative.
Frequent remembrance in battle has no material relation to the focus's sign or majority rejection.
Natural diversity is a sign for those who remember, but it has little connection to the focus's narrative nonbelief.
The believers' trust and plea not to become a trial continue the Moses-and-Pharaoh setting with a contrasting faithful response.
Competition for abundance does not illuminate the focus's sign or the majority's unbelief.
The destruction narratives are a sign for those who fear the Last Day, paralleling the focus's retrospective warning.
This repeated companion declaration affirms the Lord's might and mercy after the same sign-and-nonbelief closure.
Pharaoh's people preclassify every sign as magic and refuse belief, a direct explanation of the resistance summarized in the focus.
It identifies a concrete sign whose force is conditional on belief, but it does not develop the focus's rejection pattern.
A believers' prayer for forgiveness does not bear on the focus's sign or majority nonbelief.
The warning that punishment is not secure does not concern signs or their reception.
Reviving earth is a sign for listeners, a general receptivity parallel without the focus's narrative conflict.
Comprehensive denial of God's signs followed by seizure directly develops the accountability implicit in the focus's nonbelief.
It asks what message people could believe after this one, directly articulating persistent refusal after sufficient signs.
Most people believing in jinn concerns misdirected worship rather than the focus's response to a visible sign.
This repeated companion declaration reaffirms the Mighty and Merciful Lord after the same narrative closure.
Repeated calls for destruction in the Fire do not clarify the focus's sign or majority response.
It defines a reminder as effective for one who listens attentively, helping explain why the focus's sign does not compel all.
Mass diversion by Satan does not materially connect to the focus's narrated sign.
Its principle of affliction and pardon does not address signs or majority unbelief.
A provision is called a sign for those who reason, offering only a general sign-and-reception parallel.
This repeated companion declaration again identifies the Lord as Mighty and Merciful after the closure formula.
It describes security for believing righteous people but does not illuminate the focus's evidence or nonbelief.
Jesus presents multiple signs from God whose recognition is tied to belief, a substantial but different sign-reception parallel.
This repeated companion declaration reinforces the focus's immediate reversal of claimed power toward the Mighty and Merciful Lord.
A pressured claim of belief during punishment contrasts with the durable belief absent from the focus's majority.
Agricultural provision is a sign for reflection, a broad example of evidence requiring a receptive response.
The Pharaoh magicians invoke Pharaoh's might immediately before Moses's sign overturns their display, directly framing the focus's title reversal.
It names belief in the Lord's signs as the positive response precisely absent from the focus's majority.
A witnessed military encounter is called a sign for those with sight, supporting the focus's claim that events can function as evidence.
Witnessing persecution of believers does not clarify the focus's sign or majority nonbelief.
The created world and threatened punishment are signs for a repentant servant, only broadly related to the focus.
Wisdom and abundant good do not concern a sign being met by nonbelief.
The bee's provision is a sign for reflection, a generic example of evidence without the focus's majority contrast.
Abundant fruit in Paradise has no material relation to the focus's sign or rejection.
Calling a replaced sign fabrication shows a mechanism of rejecting revelation, though it lacks the focus's specific narrative closure.
It introduces clear verses of the book in another Moses-and-Pharaoh account, linking the focus's narrative sign to disclosed revelation.
Even overwhelming extraordinary evidence would not make the resistant believe, directly explaining why the focus's visible sign does not persuade the majority.
Turning away after being reminded of God's signs directly names the culpable response summarized as nonbelief in the focus.
Clear proof, a witness, Moses's book, belief, and the statement that most people do not believe closely parallel the focus's evidentiary contrast.
Calling the truth's bearer mad shows how hostility can recast a message rather than answer it, akin to labeling signs evasively.
Pharaoh's preserved body is explicitly made a sign for later people while many remain heedless, a direct continuation of the focus's Pharaoh sign motif.
The prophetic example and frequent remembrance do not materially clarify the focus's sign or majority nonbelief.
It contrasts believers with a mostly corrupt group, but does not develop signs or the focus's narrative evidence.
Moses and Aaron bring God's signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, who respond with arrogance; this is the focus's narrative conflict in direct form.
Rules of communal precedence and kinship do not concern the focus's sign or its reception.
Abundant fruit in Paradise does not illuminate the focus's sign or majority nonbelief.
It calls revelation true while observing that most people do not believe, directly reinforcing the focus's separation of truth from majority reception.
The ordered heavens are explained signs for people who know, a general evidence parallel without the focus's rejection theme.
An event is made a sign for believers, but the promise and gains do not illuminate the focus's majority nonbelief.
It shows that majority belief can remain compromised by association, qualifying the apparent opposition between belief and unbelief in the focus.
Failure to believe in God, the prophet, and revelation is related, but the verse lacks the focus's sign-centered majority contrast.
It explicitly says signs and warnings do not benefit people who will not believe, directly explaining the focus's distinction between sign and faith.
Clear signs and sanctuary safety do not address the focus's narrative rejection by a majority.
Sleep and death are signs for people who reflect, a generic example of evidence needing receptive thought.
Human creation and lifespan under divine knowledge do not materially clarify the focus's sign or nonbelief.
The affirmation of certain truth does not address signs or majority reception.
It connects persistent transgression with a settled state of nonbelief, offering a general account of the focus's majority response.
The Fire as a wrongdoers' outcome lacks a stated link to signs or belief in this verse.
It calls people to consider creation and asks what discourse they could believe afterward, directly challenging delayed response to available signs.
It links rejection of God's signs to humiliation and wrongdoing, supplying a related consequence with a different historical setting.
The warning against betrayal of trusts does not clarify the focus's sign or majority nonbelief.
A requested heavenly table is made a sign for all generations, but the verse says nothing about rejecting it.
Future signs will be shown and recognized while deeds remain accountable, extending the focus's concern with recognizing evidence.
The separation of idolaters from their alleged partners does not directly address signs or majority nonbelief.
The heavens and earth contain signs for believers, reinforcing that signs are received as such by believers rather than by mere majority.
It immediately precedes the focus by naming the messenger's grief that people do not become believers, establishing the majority-nonbelief problem the closure states.
It directly contrasts the focus's non-compelling sign with a hypothetical overwhelming sign that would force submission, showing that belief is not produced by spectacle alone.
It states that each new reminder is met by turning away, supplying the recurrent rejection that grounds the focus's majority nonbelief.
It explicitly says they denied and will learn the reality of what they mocked, providing the rejection-and-consequence sequence summarized by the focus.
The earth's many noble kinds are the immediate referent of the focus's statement that in that is a sign.
Every sign from their Lord is met by turning away, a direct general formulation of the response the focus records.
It depicts hearers who cannot understand the Quran and dismiss its signs as ancient tales, giving a concrete mechanism for resistant reception.
It distinguishes the messenger's pain from the wrongdoers' actual act of rejecting God's signs, directly clarifying responsibility for nonbelief.
It says that the arrogant see every sign yet do not believe in it, closely explaining why visible evidence and majority belief remain independent.
It treats earlier signs and their denial as a historical warning, supporting the focus's use of a sign-bearing narrative without duplicating its formula.
It names turning away after reminder by the Lord's signs and forgetting prior deeds, directly describing the culpable response behind the focus's nonbelief.
Moses and Aaron are told that punishment is for whoever denies and turns away, directly framing the response to their announced signs.
It states that Pharaoh was shown all the signs and nevertheless denied and refused, an exact narrative counterpart to the focus's Pharaoh setting.
Pharaoh dismisses Moses's evidence as magic used to expel them, supplying the specific evasive classification behind his refusal.
Pharaoh answers the sign by promising rival magic, showing how resistance replaces assessment of evidence with a contest of power.
It asks whether God's verses had been recited to them and then denied, directly paralleling the focus's sign-and-nonbelief charge.
Moses's offer to bring a clear sign begins the very confrontation whose rejection the focus condenses into its narrative closure.
The staff becoming a manifest serpent is a central visible sign in the Pharaoh narrative that the focus retrospectively marks as evidence.
The shining hand is the second manifest sign in the same confrontation, completing the immediate evidentiary display.
Pharaoh labels the manifest sign-bearer a skilled magician, directly showing the recoding of evidence that enables nonbelief.
The magicians' belief in the Lord of the worlds supplies a contrasting positive response to the signs within the same narrative.
Clear signs come to Pharaoh's people, who call them manifest magic, closely matching the rejection mechanism relevant to the focus.
They deny the signs despite inward certainty through injustice and arrogance, directly explaining nonbelief as moral refusal rather than insufficient evidence.
When Moses brings clear signs, Pharaoh's court calls them fabricated magic, a close parallel to the focus's sign-and-rejection setting.
No sign comes to them without their turning away, directly restating the recurrent response behind the focus's majority contrast.
When Moses shows Pharaoh's people the sign, they laugh at it, adding a direct narrative instance of dismissive reception.
Seeing a sign yet turning away and calling it continuous magic is one of the clearest general parallels to the focus's separation of visible sign from belief.
Clear signs are sent down, yet only the defiantly disobedient reject them, directly linking evidentiary clarity with culpable refusal.
It asks why the People of the Book disbelieve in God's signs while witnessing them, directly confronting belief's failure before available evidence.
Those who deny and arrogantly reject God's signs are assigned to the Fire, supplying a closely related consequence of the focus's nonbelief.
It states that those upon whom the Lord's word has become due will not believe, giving a direct general counterpart to the focus's majority statement.
Even every sign would not make them believe before the painful punishment, sharply separating abundance of evidence from faith.
The demand for a further sign is answered by locating signs under God's control, exposing the demand for spectacle rather than response to what is present.
It explicitly concerns those who do not believe in God's signs and states the consequence of their refusal.
It identifies disbelief in God's signs as the cause of the stated recompense, extending the focus's nonbelief into judgment.
The respondent is told that God's signs came and were forgotten, directly joining received evidence with accountable disregard.
People turn away from the signs in the protected sky, a direct general formulation of refusal to attend to visible evidence.
It pairs disbelief with denial of God's signs and a humiliating punishment, a close consequence parallel to the focus.
God's verses were recited to them and they turned on their heels, directly naming the response summarized by the focus's nonbelief.
Despite repeated distribution as a reminder, most people persist in refusal, closely echoing the focus's majority contrast.
It identifies disbelief in God's signs as the defining loss-making response to revelation, though without the focus's narrative closure.
The demand for signs is redirected to God while the messenger's task is clear warning, clarifying that signs are not at human command.
The evil outcome follows from denying and mocking God's signs, supplying a related rejection-to-consequence pattern.
When God's verses are recited, the hearer turns away arrogantly as though he had not heard, directly describing resistant reception.
Earlier communities denied despite messengers bringing clear proofs, scriptures, and illuminating books, a broad historical counterpart to the focus.
Disputing God's signs without authority is linked to arrogance and the sealing of hearts, explaining a resistant disposition toward evidence.
When clear verses are recited, the deniers answer only with a demand to revive ancestors, directly showing evasion rather than belief.
Clear verses are dismissed as manifest magic when recited, closely matching the Pharaoh narrative's recoding of signs.
